dataset.input:
EXCERPT from a Share Purchase Agreement governed by Nigerian law:

'Clause 8.1: The Seller warrants that the Company's financial statements for the financial year ended 31 December 2022 fairly present the financial position of the Company in all material respects.

Clause 8.2: The Seller warrants that there are no material litigation proceedings pending or threatened against the Company other than as disclosed in Schedule 3.

Clause 8.3: The Seller warrants that since 31 December 2022, there has been no material adverse change in the business, financial condition, or operations of the Company.

Clause 11.1: The aggregate liability of the Seller for all claims under this Agreement shall not exceed the Purchase Price of N500,000,000.

Clause 11.2: The Seller shall have no liability for any claim under this Agreement unless the Buyer gives written notice of the claim within 18 months from the Completion Date.

Clause 12.1: This Agreement contains the entire agreement between the parties and supersedes all prior negotiations, representations, and agreements relating to its subject matter.'

Based on this excerpt, identify: (1) the types of warranties given by the Seller; (2) what limitations on the Seller's liability are imposed; and (3) the effect of Clause 12.1 on pre-contractual representations made during negotiations.
dataset.target:
(1) Types of warranties: The Seller gives three categories of warranties: (a) financial warranty (Clause 8.1) — that the historical financial statements are accurate; (b) litigation warranty (Clause 8.2) — no undisclosed litigation exists; (c) MAC (Material Adverse Change) warranty (Clause 8.3) — no material adverse change has occurred since the last financial year-end. These are 'transaction warranties' that give the Buyer the right to claim damages if any of them are untrue at completion. The MAC warranty is forward-looking and covers the period between the last financial statements and completion.

(2) Limitations on liability: Two limitations: (a) monetary cap (Clause 11.1) — the Seller's total liability is capped at the Purchase Price (N500,000,000), which is standard in Nigerian M&A practice. The Seller cannot be required to pay more than the total consideration; (b) time limitation (Clause 11.2) — the Buyer must give notice of any claim within 18 months of completion. Claims notified after this period are time-barred. These limitations are typical and are generally enforceable under Nigerian law, subject to the public policy test.

(3) Effect of Entire Agreement Clause (12.1): This is a 'whole agreement' or 'entire agreement' clause. Under Nigerian law, it operates to: (a) exclude liability for pre-contractual representations that are not incorporated into the written agreement; (b) prevent a party from relying on oral statements or earlier drafts as contractual terms; (c) limit claims to breach of the written contract rather than misrepresentation. However, an entire agreement clause cannot exclude liability for fraud under Nigerian law — if a representation was made fraudulently, the entire agreement clause does not protect the Seller. The clause also does not prevent claims for misrepresentation under the Misrepresentation Act (applicable as received English law) unless it satisfies the reasonableness test under the applicable statute.
dataset.source: Nigerian common law of contract; Misrepresentation Act (English law received)
